scenes.text: Wild turkeys can fly, and they can hit about fifty five miles per hour.
They usually fly only short distances, but on the ground they can also run about twenty five miles per hour.
When danger comes, females tend to fly away, while males tend to run.
At sundown, they fly up into trees and climb branch by branch to a high roost, where they sleep.
A male's bare head can change color in seconds when he gets excited, turning red, white or even blue.
That fleshy flap hanging from his beak is called a snood.
One study found that females prefer males with long snoods.
A male's gobble can be heard a mile or more away.
Each wild turkey has around five to six thousand feathers.
In winter, flocks can grow to more than two hundred turkeys.
And chicks, called poults, can leave the nest within a day of hatching.
In the early nineteen hundreds, only about thirty thousand wild turkeys were left.
Thanks to restoration efforts, there are now about seven million.
Even their poop is different: males make spiral shapes, females make J shapes.
Did you know wild turkeys could fly that fast?

title: Wild turkeys can fly at 55 mph 🦃
caption: Wild turkeys fly up to about 55 mph in short bursts, run about 25 mph and sleep in trees. Their numbers went from about 30,000 to about 7 million.
